57748.e: The Colosseum was the largest amphitheatre in the Roman Empire. Estimates suggest about 50,000 seats.
57748.m: About 50,000 people could sit in the Colosseum.

57749.q: Which of the New Seven Wonders of the World is in Europe?
57749.e: The Colosseum in Rome is the only one of the New Seven Wonders in Europe. The others are in Asia and America.
57749.m: The Colosseum is the only European building among the new wonders.

57750.q: What was the Colosseum in Rome mainly used for?
57750.e: Gladiator fights and animal hunts took place in the Colosseum. The fights were meant to entertain the people.
57750.m: Gladiators fought in front of thousands of spectators in the Colosseum.

57751.q: How many of the New Seven Wonders of the World are in America?
57751.e: In America there are Christ the Redeemer in Brazil, Machu Picchu in Peru and Chichén Itzá in Mexico.
57751.m: Three of the new wonders are in America.

57752.q: Which monument was given a place of honour alongside the new wonders in the 2007 vote?
57752.e: The Pyramids of Giza are the only ancient wonder still standing. That is why they were given an honorary title and were not part of the vote.
57752.m: The Pyramids of Giza hold an honorary title among the new wonders.

57753.q: Which organisation keeps the World Heritage List?
57753.e: UNESCO is a United Nations organisation for education, science and culture. It decides which places go on the World Heritage List.
57753.m: UNESCO keeps the World Heritage List.

57754.q: What does it mean when a place is a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
a: It is especially valuable and should be protected
You are no longer allowed to visit it
Nobody is allowed to live there any more
57754.e: World Heritage Sites are important for all of humanity. The country promises to protect and preserve them. You can still visit most of them.
57754.m: World Heritage is especially valuable and is protected.

57755.q: Which three kinds of World Heritage Sites does UNESCO distinguish?
57755.e: There is cultural heritage such as buildings, natural heritage such as landscapes, and mixed sites that combine both.
57755.m: World Heritage can be cultural, natural or both at once.

57756.q: What can happen if a World Heritage Site is badly protected?
a: It can lose its World Heritage title
It is moved to another country
57756.e: UNESCO can take the title away from a site. This happened, for example, in 2009 to the Dresden Elbe Valley, because a large bridge was built there.
57756.m: A World Heritage title can be taken away again.

57757.q: What is the list for especially threatened World Heritage Sites called?
a: List of World Heritage in Danger
57757.e: The List of World Heritage in Danger, often called the ‘Red List’, contains sites threatened by war, building projects or natural disasters, for example.
57757.m: Threatened sites go on the List of World Heritage in Danger.

57758.q: Which World Heritage Site in Switzerland is a natural site?
57758.e: In 2001 the Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch region became the first natural World Heritage Site in the Alps. It includes the largest glacier in the Alps.
57758.m: Jungfrau-Aletsch is a natural heritage site in Switzerland.

57759.q: Which town in Ticino is on the World Heritage List for its three castles?
57759.e: In the Middle Ages the castles Castelgrande, Montebello and Sasso Corbaro guarded the route to the Alpine passes. They have been World Heritage since 2000.
57759.m: The three castles of Bellinzona are World Heritage.

57760.q: Which World Heritage Site does Switzerland share with five other countries around the Alps?
57760.e: The pile dwellings around the Alps have been World Heritage since 2011. The sites are in Switzerland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy and Slovenia.
57760.m: The pile dwellings are a shared World Heritage Site of six Alpine countries.

57761.q: How were the Galápagos Islands discovered in 1535?
a: A ship drifted there by chance when the wind dropped
An explorer was searching for giant tortoises
Fishermen saw the smoke of a volcano
A whale led sailors to the islands
57761.e: The Bishop of Panama was on his way to Peru when his ship drifted off course in a calm. That is how he reached the islands, which were uninhabited at the time, in 1535.
57761.m: The Galápagos Islands were discovered by chance in 1535.

57763.q: Roughly how many larger islands make up the Galápagos Islands?
57763.e: The group is made up of about 13 larger islands and many small islands and rocks. Only a few of them are inhabited.
57763.m: The Galápagos Islands are made up of about 13 larger islands.

57764.q: Why are many animals on the Galápagos hardly afraid of people?
a: For a long time they had no enemies
57764.e: On the remote islands there were no people and hardly any predators for a long time. That is why many animals do not run away when visitors come.
57764.m: Without enemies, the animals on the Galápagos never learned to be shy.

57765.q: Which introduced animals ate the plants bare on the Galápagos and were removed from several islands?
57765.e: Sailors brought goats to the islands, and they multiplied fast. They ate the giant tortoises’ food, so they were removed from several islands.
57765.m: Introduced goats threatened nature on the Galápagos.

57766.q: Which lizard on the Galápagos likes eating the fruit of prickly pear cacti?
57766.e: The yellowish land iguanas live on dry islands. They eat cactus fruit and pads and also get water that way.
57766.m: Land iguanas on the Galápagos eat cactus fruit.

57767.q: What does the old Spanish word ‘galápago’, which gave the islands their name, mean?
57767.e: The sailors named the islands after the giant tortoises that live there. These animals can live for more than 100 years.
57767.m: The Galápagos Islands are named after their giant tortoises.

57768.q: Which sea mammal often lies on beaches and even on park benches on the Galápagos?
57768.e: Galápagos sea lions are very numerous and not very shy. In the harbour towns they sometimes sleep on benches and jetties.
57768.m: Sea lions can be seen everywhere on the Galápagos.

57769.q: Which big cat of the Serengeti often drags its prey up a tree?
57769.e: The leopard is very strong and a good climber. Up in the tree its prey is safe from lions and hyenas.
57769.m: The leopard hides its prey in trees.

57770.q: Which two seasons shape life in the Serengeti?
57770.e: Near the equator there is no cold winter. What matters is whether it rains and grass grows, or whether it is dry.
57770.m: In the Serengeti the rainy season and the dry season take turns.

57771.q: Which large birds circle over dead animals in the Serengeti and eat carrion?
57771.e: Vultures spot carcasses from great heights. They eat the carrion and so help keep the savannah clean.
57771.m: Vultures are the clean-up crew of the Serengeti.

57772.q: Which animal has become especially rare in the Serengeti because of poaching?
57772.e: Poachers kill rhinos for their horn. That is why the black rhino is threatened with extinction and closely guarded.
57772.m: The black rhino has become very rare in the Serengeti.

57773.q: Which animal uses its long tongue to eat the leaves of thorny acacias?
57773.e: Thanks to its long neck, the giraffe reaches high branches. With its tongue, up to 50 centimetres long, it plucks the leaves from between the thorns.
57773.m: Giraffes eat acacia leaves with their long tongue.

57774.q: Which animal is NOT one of Africa’s ‘Big Five’?
57774.e: The ‘Big Five’ are the lion, leopard, elephant, rhino and Cape buffalo. The term comes from big-game hunters.
57774.m: The giraffe is not one of the Big Five.

57775.q: Which animals spend the day in the rivers of the Serengeti and graze on land at night?
57775.e: During the day, hippos protect themselves from the sun in the water. At night they go on land and eat huge amounts of grass.
57775.m: Hippos rest in the water by day and graze at night.

57776.q: Which mountain range is Machu Picchu in?
57776.e: Machu Picchu lies at about 2400 metres in the Andes in Peru. The Andes are the longest mountain range on Earth.
57776.m: Machu Picchu lies high in the Andes.

57777.q: In which country is Machu Picchu?
57777.e: Machu Picchu is in Peru, not far from the city of Cusco. Cusco used to be the capital of the Inca Empire.

57778.q: Why has Machu Picchu been so well preserved?
57778.e: The Spanish conquerors destroyed many Inca cities. They apparently never found Machu Picchu, so it remained largely undamaged.
57778.m: Machu Picchu was spared because the Spanish did not find it.

57779.q: What kind of World Heritage is Machu Picchu?
57779.e: Machu Picchu was recognised both for its buildings and for its special mountain forest landscape. That is why it counts as a mixed site.
57779.m: Machu Picchu is cultural and natural heritage at the same time.

57780.q: What does the name Machu Picchu mean in the Quechua language?
57780.e: In Quechua, machu means old and picchu means mountain or peak. Quechua was the language of the Incas and is still spoken in Peru today.

57781.q: Why may only a limited number of people visit Machu Picchu each day?
a: Because it is only open at night
Because the train is very small
57781.e: Lots of tourists come every day, and that damages the paths and walls. That is why there are tickets with fixed times and maximum numbers.
57781.m: Visitor numbers are limited to protect Machu Picchu.

57782.q: Which heavenly body did the Incas at Machu Picchu especially worship?
57782.e: The sun god Inti was the most important god for the Incas. At Machu Picchu there are buildings they used to watch the path of the sun.

57783.q: What is the famous trail called that you can hike over several days to Machu Picchu?
57783.e: The Inca Trail leads over passes and past old ruins all the way to Machu Picchu. The hike usually takes four days.
57783.m: You hike to Machu Picchu on the Inca Trail.

57784.q: Who lived in the caves of Petra until the 1980s?
57784.e: A Bedouin tribe lived in the old rock caves. When Petra became World Heritage, the families moved to a new village nearby.
57784.m: Bedouins lived in the caves of Petra for a long time.

57785.q: What badly damaged many buildings in Petra in AD 363?
57785.e: In AD 363 a strong earthquake destroyed many free-standing buildings and water pipes. After that the city became less and less important.
57785.m: An earthquake hit Petra hard in the year 363.

57786.q: What colour is the rock that Petra was carved from?
57786.e: Petra’s sandstone glows in shades of red and pink. That is why Petra is also called the ‘Rose City’.
57786.m: Petra is made of reddish sandstone.

57787.q: How do you reach Petra’s famous Treasury on foot?
a: Through a tunnel under the sea
57787.e: A narrow rocky gorge more than a kilometre long leads into Petra. At the end, the Treasury suddenly appears.
57787.m: A narrow gorge leads into Petra.

57788.q: What did Bedouins shoot at on the façade of the Treasury, because they thought there was gold in it?
57788.e: According to legend, a treasure was hidden in the urn at the top of the façade. The bullet holes can still be seen today, but the urn is solid stone.
57788.m: The urn on the Treasury is full of bullet holes, but empty.

57789.q: How did Johann Ludwig Burckhardt from Basel travel through Arabia without standing out?
a: As a soldier with an army
57789.e: Burckhardt learned Arabic and wore Arab clothing. That way he was able to reach Petra without being recognised.
57789.m: Burckhardt travelled through Arabia in disguise.

57790.q: Which modern script developed from the script of the Nabataeans?
57790.e: The Nabataeans wrote in their own script. Over time, the Arabic script developed from it.
57790.m: Arabic script comes from the script of the Nabataeans.

57791.q: In which country is the temple city of Angkor?
57791.e: Angkor is in the north-west of Cambodia. The nearest town is Siem Reap.

57792.q: Which empire had its capital at Angkor?
57792.e: From the 9th to the 15th century, Angkor was the centre of the Khmer Empire. It was one of the largest cities of its time.
57792.m: Angkor was the capital of the Khmer Empire.

57793.q: What did Angkor look like when European explorers visited it around 1860?
57793.e: After the end of the Khmer Empire, the forest grew over many temples. The Frenchman Henri Mouhot made Angkor famous in Europe with his reports.
57793.m: Angkor was overgrown by jungle for a long time.

57794.q: Where can Angkor Wat be seen as a symbol?
57794.e: The flag of Cambodia shows the outline of Angkor Wat in white. Hardly any other country has a building on its flag.
57794.m: Angkor Wat appears on the flag of Cambodia.

57795.q: What is the walled royal city at Angkor called, with the Bayon in its centre?
57795.e: Angkor Thom means ‘great city’. King Jayavarman VII had it surrounded with a wall and gates around 1200.
57795.m: Angkor Thom is the great royal city of Angkor.

57796.q: What can be seen on the towers of the Bayon temple at Angkor?
57796.e: The Bayon is famous for more than 200 huge, smiling stone faces on its towers. It is not quite certain who they represent.
57796.m: The Bayon temple is known for its smiling stone faces.

57797.q: Which large lake nearby supplied Angkor with fish and water?
57797.e: The Tonle Sap is the largest lake in Southeast Asia. A clever system of canals and reservoirs used its water for growing rice.
57797.m: The Tonle Sap lake was vital for Angkor.

57798.q: In which country is Chartres Cathedral?
57798.e: Chartres lies about 80 kilometres south-west of Paris. The cathedral towers over the small town and can be seen from far away.

57799.q: In which architectural style was Chartres Cathedral built?
57799.e: The cathedral is a major Gothic work with pointed arches and flying buttresses. This way of building allows tall walls with large windows.
57799.m: Chartres Cathedral is a masterpiece of Gothic architecture.

57800.q: What is Chartres Cathedral especially famous for?
57800.e: Chartres has one of the largest collections of medieval stained glass windows. Many of them still date from the 13th century.
57800.m: The medieval stained glass windows of Chartres are world-famous.

57801.q: Which colour shines especially beautifully in many of the stained glass windows of Chartres Cathedral?
57801.e: The bright blue of the windows is so famous that it is called ‘Chartres blue’. Exactly how it was made is still not fully understood.
57801.m: The windows of Chartres are famous for their bright blue.

57802.q: What is set into the floor of the nave at Chartres?
57802.e: The 13th-century labyrinth is almost 13 metres across. Believers walk the path to the centre as a prayer.
57802.m: There is a labyrinth in the floor of Chartres Cathedral.

57803.q: What is striking about the two west towers of Chartres Cathedral?
a: They are the same height and identical
57803.e: The south tower is plain and older, while the north tower later got a decorated late Gothic spire. That is why the towers look different.
57803.m: The two towers of Chartres are designed differently.

57804.q: Which event in 1194 led to Chartres Cathedral being rebuilt?
57804.e: In 1194 a fire almost completely destroyed the old church. The new building was largely finished in only about 30 years.
57804.m: After a fire in 1194, Chartres was rebuilt.

57805.q: Who is Chartres Cathedral dedicated to?
57805.e: The cathedral is called Notre-Dame de Chartres, meaning ‘Our Lady’. It keeps a cloth that is honoured as Mary’s robe.
57805.m: Chartres Cathedral is dedicated to Mary.

57806.q: Which parliament building stands on the edge of Bern’s Old Town?
57806.e: The National Council and the Council of States meet in the Federal Palace. It was completed in 1902 and stands high above the River Aare.
57806.m: The Federal Palace stands on the edge of Bern’s Old Town.

57807.q: Where do Bern’s bears live today on the bank of the River Aare?
57807.e: Since 2009 the bears have lived in the Bear Park on the slope by the Aare. The old bear pit next to it is still part of it.
57807.m: Bern’s bears live in the Bear Park by the Aare.

57808.q: Which ruling family founded the city of Bern in 1191?
57808.e: Duke Berthold V of Zähringen founded Bern in 1191. The Zähringen family also founded Fribourg.
57808.m: Bern was founded in 1191 by the Zähringen family.

57809.q: What is the famous tower with an astronomical clock in Bern’s Old Town called?
57809.e: The Zytglogge was once a city gate. The astronomical clock with its moving figures dates from 1530.
57809.m: The Zytglogge has been telling the time since 1530.

57810.q: Roughly how long are the arcades of Bern’s Old Town?
57810.e: The arcades are covered walkways under the houses. At about 6 kilometres long, you can shop for a long time in Bern without getting wet.
57810.m: Bern’s arcades are about 6 kilometres long.

57811.q: How tall is the tower of Bern Minster, the tallest church tower in Switzerland?
57811.e: The Minster tower is about 100.6 metres tall. It was only finished in 1893, more than 450 years after building began.
57811.m: The tower of Bern Minster is the tallest church tower in Switzerland.

57812.q: What is the Bern fountain called whose figure is eating a child?
57812.e: The Child Eater Fountain on Kornhausplatz dates from the 16th century. What the figure really means is still unclear.
57812.m: The Child Eater Fountain is Bern’s strangest fountain.

57813.q: What material were the houses mainly built of after the city fire of 1405?
57813.e: After the great fire of 1405, people in Bern built with sandstone instead of wood. The greenish-grey stone still shapes the Old Town today.
57813.m: Bern’s Old Town is built of sandstone.

57814.q: Which famous physicist lived at Kramgasse 49 in Bern’s Old Town?
57814.e: Albert Einstein lived at Kramgasse 49 from 1903 to 1905. His special theory of relativity was created there in 1905.
57814.m: Albert Einstein lived in Bern’s Old Town.

57815.q: In which canton is the Lavaux wine region?
57815.e: Lavaux is in the canton of Vaud on the northern shore of Lake Geneva. The vineyards rise steeply from the lakeshore.
57815.m: Lavaux is in the canton of Vaud.

57816.e: The vineyard terraces of Lavaux stretch along Lake Geneva. In French the lake is called Lac Léman.
57816.m: The vineyard terraces of Lavaux are on Lake Geneva.

57817.q: Between which towns does Lavaux stretch?
57817.e: Lavaux runs along about 30 kilometres of shore between Lausanne and the area around Vevey and Montreux.
57817.m: Lavaux lies between Lausanne and Vevey.

57818.q: How are the vineyards in Lavaux laid out?
a: On steep terraces with stone walls
57818.e: As early as the Middle Ages, monks built terraces with stone walls on the steep slopes above Lake Geneva. Today there are about 10,000 terraces.
57818.m: In Lavaux the vines grow on steep terraces.

57819.q: Which white grape variety is mainly grown in Lavaux?
57819.e: The Chasselas grape shapes winegrowing in Lavaux. It is the typical white wine grape of western Switzerland.
57819.m: Chasselas is the main grape variety in Lavaux.

57820.q: Which three ‘suns’ are said to warm the grapes in Lavaux?
57820.e: The grapes get direct sunlight, light reflected from the lake and warmth from the stone walls. People speak of the ‘three suns’.
57820.m: Sun, lake and warm walls are the three suns of Lavaux.

57821.q: Which list has Lavaux been on since 2007?
a: List of the new wonders of the world
57821.e: The vineyard terraces of Lavaux became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2007. They show how people have shaped a landscape over centuries.

57822.q: Between which places does the Rhaetian Railway’s World Heritage line run?
57822.e: The Albula line runs from Thusis to St Moritz, and the Bernina line continues to Tirano in Italy. Together they have been World Heritage since 2008.
57822.m: The World Heritage line runs from Thusis to Tirano.

57823.q: Which country does Switzerland share the Albula/Bernina World Heritage Site with?
57823.e: The Bernina line ends in Tirano in Italy. That is why the World Heritage Site is shared by Switzerland and Italy.
57823.m: Switzerland shares the railway World Heritage Site with Italy.

57824.q: Which viaduct near Filisur leads straight into a tunnel in the rock face?
57824.e: The Landwasser Viaduct is about 65 metres high. At the end, the train goes straight into a tunnel in the vertical rock face.
57824.m: The Landwasser Viaduct ends right in a rock tunnel.

57825.q: Which structure on the Bernina line makes the train go round in a circle and pass under itself?
57825.e: At the Brusio Spiral Viaduct, the train goes round a loop and passes underneath itself. That way it climbs a lot of height over a short distance.
57825.m: At the Brusio Spiral Viaduct the train goes round a loop.

57826.q: Roughly how high does the Bernina Railway climb at its highest point?
57826.e: At Ospizio Bernina the railway reaches 2253 metres above sea level. It is the highest point of any Alpine crossing by ordinary railway without a cogwheel.
57826.m: The Bernina Railway climbs over 2000 metres high.

57827.q: What track gauge does the Rhaetian Railway have?
57827.e: The Rhaetian Railway runs on metre gauge, so the rails are one metre apart. Narrow gauges allow tighter bends in the mountains.
57827.m: The Rhaetian Railway runs on metre gauge.

57828.q: What does the Bernina Railway manage even though it has no cogwheel?
57828.e: The Bernina Railway climbs up to 7 metres over 100 metres of track. That makes it one of the steepest railways in the world without a cogwheel.
57828.m: The Bernina Railway runs very steeply without a cogwheel.

57829.q: How does the Albula line near Bergün climb a lot of height over a short distance?
57829.e: Between Bergün and Preda the line turns in spiral tunnels and loops. That way the gradient stays gentle despite the big difference in height.
57829.m: Spiral tunnels help the Albula line gain height.

57830.q: Roughly how long did Columbus’s first crossing from the Canary Islands to the first island in America take?
57830.e: The ships left the Canary island of La Gomera on 6 September and reached an island in the Bahamas on 12 October. That is 36 days, so about five weeks.
57830.m: Columbus’s first Atlantic crossing took about five weeks.

57831.q: What was the name of Columbus’s largest ship (the flagship) on his first voyage?
57831.e: The Santa María was the flagship of the first voyage. It ran aground off the island of Hispaniola at Christmas 1492.
57831.m: Columbus’s flagship was called the Santa María.

57832.q: Which two smaller ships went with Columbus in 1492 alongside the flagship?
57832.e: The fleet was made up of the Santa María and the two smaller caravels, the Niña and the Pinta.
57832.m: The Niña and the Pinta sailed with Columbus in 1492.

57833.q: Which country paid for Columbus’s first voyage?
57833.e: The Spanish royal couple, Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon, supported the voyage after Portugal had said no.
57833.m: Columbus sailed on behalf of the Spanish crown.

57834.q: According to what we know today, which city did Christopher Columbus probably come from?
57834.e: Most researchers believe that Columbus was born around 1451 in the port city of Genoa in Italy.

57835.q: Which destination did Columbus want to reach when he sailed west?
57835.e: Columbus wanted to find a sea route westwards to the spice lands of Asia. That is why he called the people of America ‘Indians’.
57835.m: Columbus was looking for a sea route west to Asia.

57836.q: On which group of islands did Columbus first go ashore in 1492?
57836.e: On 12 October 1492 Columbus reached an island in the Bahamas. He named it San Salvador, ‘Holy Saviour’.
57836.m: In 1492 Columbus first landed in the Bahamas.

57837.q: How many voyages to America did Christopher Columbus make altogether?
57837.e: Between 1492 and 1504 Columbus sailed across the Atlantic to the Caribbean and Central America four times.
57837.m: Columbus sailed to America four times altogether.

57838.q: What did Columbus believe until his death in 1506 about the lands he had discovered?
57838.e: Columbus was convinced he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. It was Amerigo Vespucci who spread the idea of a ‘New World’.
57838.m: Columbus thought all his life that America was part of Asia.

57839.q: Which sea route did Vasco da Gama find as the first European?
57839.e: Vasco da Gama sailed from Portugal round Africa to India and returned the same way. This created a direct sea link to Asia.
57839.m: Vasco da Gama found the sea route to India.

57840.q: Which country did Vasco da Gama come from?
57840.e: Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese navigator. He sailed on behalf of King Manuel I of Portugal.

57841.q: In which year did Vasco da Gama reach India?
57841.e: In May 1498 Vasco da Gama landed on the south-west coast of India, almost a year after setting off.
57841.m: Vasco da Gama arrived in India in 1498.

57842.q: Which cape at the south of Africa did Vasco da Gama sail round on the way to India?
57842.e: To get round Africa, the fleet had to pass the Cape of Good Hope at the southern tip of Africa.
57842.m: The route to India went round the Cape of Good Hope.

57843.q: Which continent did Vasco da Gama sail round on the way to India?
57843.e: Vasco da Gama sailed south from Portugal along the coast of Africa, round its southern tip and then across the Indian Ocean to India.
57843.m: The sea route to India went round Africa.

57844.q: Which goods made the sea route to India especially valuable for Portugal?
57844.e: Pepper, cinnamon and other spices were very expensive in Europe. By sea, Portugal could buy them without middlemen.
57844.m: The sea route to India was valuable mainly because of spices.

57845.q: Which Portuguese navigator had already sailed round the southern tip of Africa in 1488, before Vasco da Gama?
57845.e: In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias was the first European to sail round the Cape of Good Hope. This prepared the way for Vasco da Gama’s voyage.
57845.m: In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias was the first to round the southern tip of Africa.

57846.q: Why did Vasco da Gama call a coast in present-day South Africa ‘Natal’?
57846.e: Natal is the Portuguese word for Christmas. The fleet sailed past this coast at Christmas 1497.

57847.q: What achievement is Ferdinand Magellan’s expedition famous for?
a: The first voyage round the world
The first voyage to the North Pole
57847.e: The expedition was the first to sail all the way round the Earth. However, Magellan himself did not survive the voyage.
57847.m: The Magellan expedition was the first to sail round the world.

57848.q: For which country did the Portuguese-born Magellan sail on his famous voyage?
57848.e: The Portuguese king turned down Magellan’s plan. So he went into the service of King Charles I of Spain.
57848.m: Magellan sailed on behalf of Spain.

57849.q: In which year did Magellan’s fleet set off to sail round the world?
57849.e: In September 1519 the fleet left Spain. The voyage took almost three years.
57849.m: Magellan’s voyage round the world began in 1519.

57850.q: How many ships did Magellan’s fleet set off with in 1519?
57850.e: The fleet was made up of the ships Trinidad, San Antonio, Concepción, Victoria and Santiago.
57850.m: Magellan set off in 1519 with five ships.

57851.q: What name did Magellan give the great ocean he reached after the strait?
57851.e: After the storms of the strait, the sea was calm for a long time. That is why Magellan called it ‘Mar Pacífico’, the peaceful sea.

57852.q: Where did Ferdinand Magellan die in 1521?
57852.e: In 1521 Magellan was killed in a fight with local people on the Philippine island of Mactan.
57852.m: Magellan died in the Philippines in 1521.

57853.q: How many men survived Magellan’s voyage round the world from 1519 to 1522?
57853.e: Of about 240 men who set off in 1519, only 18 came back to Spain on the last ship in 1522.
57853.m: Only a few men survived the first voyage round the world.

57854.q: How many of the five ships of Magellan’s fleet returned to Spain?
57854.e: Under the command of Juan Sebastián Elcano, only the Victoria returned to Spain in 1522.
57854.m: Only one ship completed the whole voyage round the world.

57855.q: What are the ‘Magellanic Clouds’, named after Magellan?
a: Two galaxies in the southern sky
Fog banks over Tierra del Fuego
Two groups of islands in the Pacific
57855.e: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are neighbouring galaxies of the Milky Way. You can only see them well from the southern hemisphere.
57855.m: The Magellanic Clouds are galaxies in the southern sky.

57856.q: Which country did the navigator James Cook come from?
57856.e: James Cook was born in England in 1728 and was a captain in the British navy.
57856.m: James Cook was a British navigator.

57857.q: What was the name of James Cook’s ship on his first great voyage from 1768?
57857.e: Cook sailed into the Pacific on HMS Endeavour, partly to observe the transit of Venus in 1769 on Tahiti.
57857.m: Cook’s first ship was called the Endeavour.

57858.q: Which coast of Australia did James Cook explore and map in 1770 as the first European?
57858.e: The Dutch already knew the west and north coasts. In 1770 Cook was the first European to sail along the east coast.
57858.m: In 1770 James Cook mapped the east coast of Australia.

57859.q: Why did Botany Bay near Sydney, where James Cook landed in 1770, get its name?
a: Because of the many new plants
57859.e: The scientists on Cook’s ship found a great many unknown plants there. That is why the bay was called Botany Bay.
57859.m: Cook landed at Botany Bay in 1770.

57860.q: How many great voyages of discovery to the Pacific did James Cook lead?
57860.e: Cook led three Pacific voyages: from 1768 to 1771, from 1772 to 1775 and from 1776.
57860.m: James Cook made three great voyages to the Pacific.

57861.q: Where did James Cook die in 1779?
57861.e: Cook was killed in February 1779 during a quarrel with local people at Kealakekua Bay in Hawaii.
57861.m: James Cook died in Hawaii in 1779.

57862.q: Which food did James Cook use to protect his crew from the disease scurvy?
57862.e: Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C. Among other things, Cook had his men eat sauerkraut, which contains some vitamin C.
57862.m: Cook fought scurvy with sauerkraut, among other things.

57863.q: Which line of latitude did James Cook cross in 1773 as the first known navigator?
57863.e: On his second voyage, on the Resolution, Cook crossed the Antarctic Circle in January 1773. But he never saw Antarctica itself.
57863.m: In 1773 Cook was the first to cross the Antarctic Circle.

57864.q: In which city was Alexander von Humboldt born in 1769?
57864.e: Alexander von Humboldt was born in 1769 in Berlin, which belonged to Prussia at the time.
57864.m: Alexander von Humboldt came from Berlin.

57865.q: Which continent did Alexander von Humboldt mainly explore on his great journey from 1799 to 1804?
57865.e: Humboldt travelled through what are now Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru and Mexico, and at the end visited the USA.
57865.m: From 1799 to 1804 Humboldt mainly explored South America.

57866.q: What did Alexander von Humboldt mainly collect on his journey through America?
57866.e: Humboldt and his companion, the botanist Aimé Bonpland, collected thousands of plants and described many new species.
57866.m: Humboldt collected thousands of plants in America.

57867.q: Which volcano in Ecuador did Humboldt climb in 1802 to what was then a record height?
57867.e: On Chimborazo, Humboldt reached about 5600 metres. For a long time this was the greatest height a person was known to have reached.
57867.m: In 1802 Humboldt climbed to a record height on Chimborazo.

a: A cold ocean current off South America
A river in the Amazon region
A warm wind in the Andes
57868.e: The Humboldt Current flows north off the west coast of Chile and Peru. It brings cold, nutrient-rich water.
57868.m: The Humboldt Current is a cold current off Peru and Chile.

57869.q: What is the great late work called in which Humboldt wanted to describe knowledge about the whole world?
57869.e: Humboldt’s work ‘Cosmos’, in several volumes, appeared from 1845. It was a great success.
57869.m: Humboldt’s most famous book is called Cosmos.

57870.q: What was the name of Alexander von Humboldt’s brother, who helped found the University of Berlin?
57870.e: Wilhelm von Humboldt was a linguist and education reformer. The Humboldt University in Berlin is named after both brothers.
57870.m: Wilhelm von Humboldt was the brother of the explorer Alexander.

57871.q: Which link between two large river systems did Humboldt investigate in South America in 1800?
a: Between the Orinoco and the Amazon
Between the Nile and the Congo
Between the Rhine and the Danube
Between the Mississippi and the Ohio
57871.e: Humboldt confirmed that the Casiquiare river connects the Orinoco river system with that of the Amazon.
57871.m: The Casiquiare connects the Orinoco and the Amazon.

57872.q: In which year did Roald Amundsen become the first person to reach the South Pole?
57872.e: Amundsen reached the South Pole on 14 December 1911 with four companions. Scott only arrived a month later.
57872.m: In 1911 Amundsen was the first to stand at the South Pole.

57874.q: On which ship did Amundsen head for Antarctica in 1910?
57874.e: The Fram was an especially sturdy polar ship that Fridtjof Nansen had already used.
57874.m: Amundsen sailed to Antarctica on the Fram.

57875.q: Which animals pulled the sledges on Amundsen’s South Pole expedition?
57875.e: Amundsen relied completely on experienced sledge dogs. That was an important reason for his success.
57875.m: Amundsen reached the South Pole with dog sledges.

57876.q: Which sea route in the north of America did Amundsen become the first to sail all the way through, from 1903 to 1906?
57876.e: In the small ship Gjøa, Amundsen sailed from the Atlantic through the maze of Canada’s Arctic islands to the Pacific.
57876.m: Amundsen was the first to sail through the Northwest Passage.

57877.q: In what did Amundsen fly over the North Pole in 1926?
57877.e: Together with Umberto Nobile and Lincoln Ellsworth, Amundsen flew in the airship Norge from Svalbard to Alaska over the North Pole.
57877.m: In 1926 Amundsen flew over the North Pole in the airship Norge.

57878.q: How did Roald Amundsen die in 1928?
a: On a rescue flight in the Arctic
57878.e: Amundsen flew off to search for the crew of the airship Italia, which had crashed. His plane disappeared over the Barents Sea.
57878.m: Amundsen disappeared on a rescue flight in 1928.

57879.q: Which two explorers is the research station at the South Pole named after?
57879.e: The American Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station remembers the two men who raced each other to the South Pole.
57879.m: The South Pole station bears the names Amundsen and Scott.

57880.q: Which country did the polar explorer Robert Falcon Scott come from?
57880.e: Robert Falcon Scott was an officer in the British navy and led two Antarctic expeditions.
57880.m: Robert Falcon Scott was a British polar explorer.

57881.q: When did Robert Falcon Scott and his group reach the South Pole?
57881.e: Scott and four companions arrived at the South Pole on 17 January 1912, just over a month after Amundsen.
57881.m: Scott reached the South Pole in January 1912.

57882.q: What did Scott’s group find at the South Pole?
a: A tent with a Norwegian flag
57882.e: Amundsen had left a tent with a Norwegian flag and a letter at the Pole. Scott now knew he had only come second.
57882.m: At the South Pole Scott found the traces of Amundsen.

57883.q: What happened to Scott and his companions on the way back from the South Pole?
a: They spent the winter with Amundsen
They reached their ship safe and well
57883.e: Cold, hunger and exhaustion cost all five men their lives. Scott died in his tent at the end of March 1912.
57883.m: Scott’s polar party died on the way back.

57884.q: Who reached the South Pole before Robert Falcon Scott?
57884.e: Amundsen was about a month faster. At the Pole, Scott found the tent with the Norwegian flag.
57884.m: Amundsen reached the South Pole before Scott.

57885.q: Apart from dogs, which animals did Scott mainly use to pull loads?
57885.e: Scott relied on ponies and motor sledges. The ponies did not cope well with the cold.
57885.m: Scott relied mainly on ponies and motor sledges.

57886.q: Why did one of Scott’s sick companions walk out alone into the blizzard?
a: So as not to hold the others up
57886.e: Lawrence Oates was ill and could only move slowly. In March 1912 he walked out so that the others could move faster. He did not come back.
57886.m: One of Scott’s companions sacrificed himself for his friends.

57887.q: How do we know so exactly today what happened on Scott’s last journey?
a: From his diaries, which were found
From radio messages to his ship
57887.e: A search party found the tent with the dead men in November 1912. Scott’s diary describes the journey until shortly before his death.
57887.m: Scott’s diary tells of the end of his expedition.

57888.q: Which summit did Edmund Hillary climb in 1953 as one of the first two people?
57888.e: On 29 May 1953 Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first people to stand on top of Mount Everest.
57888.m: In 1953 Hillary was one of the first to climb Mount Everest.

57889.q: Which honour did Edmund Hillary receive in 1953 after climbing Everest?
57889.e: The British Queen Elizabeth II knighted Hillary in 1953. From then on he was Sir Edmund Hillary.
57889.m: After Everest, Hillary became Sir Edmund Hillary.

57890.q: Which country did Edmund Hillary come from?
57890.e: Hillary was born in Auckland, New Zealand, in 1919. His picture is on the New Zealand 5-dollar note.
57890.m: Edmund Hillary was a New Zealander.

57891.q: What was Edmund Hillary’s job before his success on Everest?
57891.e: Hillary worked with his brother keeping bees, as a beekeeper.
57891.m: Edmund Hillary was a beekeeper by trade.

57892.q: With which famous astronaut did Hillary land a plane at the North Pole in 1985?
57892.e: In 1985 Hillary flew to the North Pole in a small plane with Neil Armstrong. In 1969 Armstrong had been the first person on the Moon.
57892.m: In 1985 Hillary flew to the North Pole with Neil Armstrong.

57893.q: Which country sent an expedition to Everest in 1952, a year before Hillary, that almost reached the summit?
57893.e: On the Swiss Everest expedition of 1952, Raymond Lambert climbed with Tenzing Norgay to about 8600 metres. That was a height record at the time.
57893.m: A Swiss expedition came very close to the summit of Everest in 1952.

57894.q: Which country organised the expedition with which Hillary climbed Everest in 1953?
57894.e: The expedition was led by the British officer John Hunt.
57894.m: The 1953 Everest expedition was a British expedition.

57895.q: Which pole did Hillary reach in 1958 with converted tractors?
57895.e: As part of a crossing of Antarctica, Hillary drove to the South Pole with tractors in 1958.
57895.m: In 1958 Hillary drove tractors to the South Pole.

57896.q: What did Edmund Hillary build in Nepal with his foundation, the Himalayan Trust?
57896.e: Hillary founded the Himalayan Trust in 1960. He helped the Sherpas with schools and hospitals.
57896.m: Hillary built schools and hospitals for the Sherpas.

57897.q: Which city did the traveller Ida Pfeiffer come from?
57897.e: Ida Pfeiffer was born in Vienna in 1797 and was Austrian.

57898.q: What is Ida Pfeiffer especially known for?
a: As a woman she travelled round the world twice
She was the first to reach the North Pole
She was the first to fly across the Atlantic
57898.e: In the 19th century Ida Pfeiffer went round the Earth twice, mostly alone and with little money. For a woman that was very unusual at the time.
57898.m: Ida Pfeiffer travelled round the world twice.

57899.q: When did Ida Pfeiffer start her great journeys?
a: When her sons were grown up
When she was ten years old
57899.e: Only at about 44, after her sons had become independent, did she set off on her first great journey in 1842.
57899.m: Ida Pfeiffer only started travelling when she was over 40.

57900.q: Where did Ida Pfeiffer’s first great journey in 1842 take her?
57900.e: Her first journey took her via Constantinople to Palestine and Egypt. She wrote a successful book about it.
57900.m: Ida Pfeiffer’s first journey went to the Holy Land.

57901.q: How did Ida Pfeiffer pay for part of her journeys?
a: With travel books and natural objects she collected
With gold from her own mines
With wages as a ship’s captain
57901.e: She wrote successful travel accounts and sold insects, plants and rocks she had collected to museums.
57901.m: Ida Pfeiffer also paid for her journeys with books and collections.

57902.q: Which island in the far north of Europe did Ida Pfeiffer travel to in 1845?
57902.e: In 1845 she travelled to Iceland and Scandinavia. She published a book about that too.
57902.m: Ida Pfeiffer travelled to Iceland in 1845.

57903.q: Which large island off Africa did Ida Pfeiffer’s last journey take her to?
57903.e: In Madagascar she fell seriously ill with fever in 1857. She died in Vienna in 1858 after returning home.
57903.m: Ida Pfeiffer’s last journey took her to Madagascar.

57904.q: Why is Ida Pfeiffer seen as a role model for later travellers?
a: As a woman she travelled alone to distant lands
She founded the first travel agency
57904.e: In the 19th century women hardly ever travelled alone. Ida Pfeiffer proved that women can make great journeys of exploration too.
57904.m: Ida Pfeiffer showed that women can travel the world alone.

57905.q: Which city did the traveller Marco Polo come from?
57905.e: Marco Polo was born around 1254 in the trading city of Venice.

57906.q: At which ruler’s court did Marco Polo live for many years?
a: At the court of Kublai Khan
At the court of the Sultan of Delhi
At the court of the Pharaoh
57906.e: Marco Polo served the Mongol Great Khan Kublai Khan, who ruled over China.
57906.m: Marco Polo lived at the court of Kublai Khan.

57907.q: Who did Marco Polo set off to Asia with in 1271?
a: With his father and his uncle
57907.e: His father Niccolò and his uncle Maffeo Polo were merchants and already knew the way to China.
57907.m: Marco Polo travelled to Asia with his father and uncle.

57908.q: Roughly how long was Marco Polo away before he returned to Venice in 1295?
57908.e: He set off in 1271 and came back in 1295. That is 24 years.
57908.m: Marco Polo was away for almost a quarter of a century.

57909.q: On which famous trade route did Marco Polo travel to China?
57909.e: The Silk Road was a network of caravan routes between the Mediterranean and China.
57909.m: Marco Polo travelled along the Silk Road.

57910.q: Where was Marco Polo’s travel account written?
a: On a ship in the Indian Ocean
57910.e: As a prisoner of war in Genoa, Marco Polo told his adventures to his fellow prisoner Rustichello da Pisa, who wrote them down.
57910.m: Marco Polo’s account was written in a prison in Genoa.

57911.q: Which later navigator is Marco Polo’s book said to have inspired to make his voyage?
57911.e: Columbus owned a copy of Marco Polo’s travel account. Its descriptions of the riches of Asia encouraged him to look for a sea route to the west.
57911.m: Marco Polo’s book inspired Columbus to make his voyage.

57912.q: Which means of payment from China did Marco Polo describe as a great novelty?
57912.e: In Europe people paid with coins. Marco Polo was amazed that in China you could pay with printed paper.
57912.m: Marco Polo told Europe about Chinese paper money.

57913.q: Which present-day country did the traveller Ibn Battuta come from?
57913.e: Ibn Battuta was born in 1304 in Tangier, in what is now Morocco.

57914.q: With what aim did Ibn Battuta begin his travels in 1325?
a: A search for gold in Africa
57914.e: As a young man he set off on the Hajj to Mecca. After that he kept travelling for almost 30 years.
57914.m: Ibn Battuta began his travels with a pilgrimage to Mecca.

57915.q: Roughly how far did Ibn Battuta travel altogether on his journeys?
57915.e: In about 30 years Ibn Battuta travelled about 120,000 kilometres, more than Marco Polo.

57916.q: How do we know about Ibn Battuta’s travels today?
57916.e: After returning home, Ibn Battuta dictated a travel account, the Rihla. The word is Arabic and means ‘journey’.
57916.m: Ibn Battuta left behind a travel account.

57917.q: Which office did Ibn Battuta hold for several years in Delhi?
57917.e: The Sultan of Delhi appointed the legal scholar Ibn Battuta as a qadi, that is, a judge.
57917.m: Ibn Battuta worked as a judge in Delhi.

57918.q: Which West African empire, with the city of Timbuktu, did Ibn Battuta visit in 1352 to 1353?
57918.e: On his last journey Ibn Battuta crossed the Sahara and visited the rich Mali Empire.
57918.m: Ibn Battuta crossed the Sahara to the Mali Empire.

57919.q: How did Ibn Battuta travel across the Indian Ocean to the Maldives in the 14th century?
57919.e: In the 14th century there were no steamships or planes. Ibn Battuta travelled on sailing ships and worked as a judge in the Maldives for about nine months.
57919.m: Ibn Battuta crossed the Indian Ocean on sailing ships.

57920.q: According to his own account, which distant country in the east did Ibn Battuta reach by sea?
57920.e: Ibn Battuta landed in the port city of Quanzhou and travelled as far as Hangzhou. Researchers doubt whether he also reached Beijing, as he claimed.
57920.m: Ibn Battuta travelled by sea as far as China.

57921.q: Which country does the adventurer Bertrand Piccard come from?
57921.e: Bertrand Piccard was born in Lausanne in 1958 and is Swiss.
57921.m: Bertrand Piccard is a Swiss adventurer.

57922.q: What did Bertrand Piccard and Brian Jones achieve in 1999?
a: The first non-stop balloon flight round the world
The first trip to the Mariana Trench
The first flight to the Moon
The first crossing of the Sahara
57922.e: In March 1999, in the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3, they were the first to go round the Earth without landing.
57922.m: In 1999 Piccard went round the Earth non-stop in a balloon.

57923.q: What drove the balloon Breitling Orbiter 3 forward on its trip round the world?
57923.e: A balloon has no engine. Piccard and Jones looked for strong winds high up, which carried them round the Earth in just under 20 days.
57923.m: A balloon is carried by the wind.

57924.q: What did the aircraft Solar Impulse 2 use to fly round the world?
57924.e: About 17,000 solar cells on the wings supplied the electricity. Batteries stored energy for the night.
57924.m: Solar Impulse flew on solar power alone.

57925.q: How could the solar aircraft Solar Impulse 2 keep flying at night?
a: With electricity from batteries charged during the day
With moonlight on the solar cells
It couldn’t, it landed every evening
57925.e: During the day the solar cells supplied more electricity than the motor needed. The rest was stored in batteries and used at night.
57925.m: At night Solar Impulse flew on electricity from batteries.

57926.q: How many people could fit in the cockpit of Solar Impulse 2?
57926.e: The cockpit had only one seat. That is why Bertrand Piccard and André Borschberg took turns flying the stages.
57926.m: There was only ever one pilot in the cockpit of Solar Impulse.

57927.q: What profession did Bertrand Piccard train for?
57927.e: Bertrand Piccard studied medicine and became a psychiatrist.
57927.m: Bertrand Piccard is a psychiatrist by profession.

57928.q: What did Bertrand Piccard’s grandfather Auguste Piccard become famous for in 1931?
a: He went up into the stratosphere in a balloon
57928.e: In 1931 Auguste Piccard was the first person to rise into the stratosphere, to about 15,800 metres, with a balloon and a pressurised capsule.
57928.m: In 1931 Auguste Piccard was the first to go up into the stratosphere.

57929.q: What did Bertrand Piccard’s father Jacques Piccard reach in 1960 in the submersible Trieste?
a: The deepest point of the ocean
The South Pole under the ice
57929.e: In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh dived in the Mariana Trench to a depth of about 10,900 metres.
57929.m: In 1960 Jacques Piccard dived into the Mariana Trench.

59611.q: A woman borrows 200 francs at 20 per cent interest a year. How much does she pay back after one year?
59611.e: Interest: 200 × 0.20 = 40 francs; she has to pay back 200 + 40 = 240 francs.
59611.m: Interest is calculated as a percentage of the amount borrowed.

62556.q: A train on a half-hourly timetable leaves at 7:14. When does the next train on this line leave?
62556.e: Half-hourly means a train leaves every 30 minutes. 7:14 plus 30 minutes is 7:44.
62556.m: On a half-hourly timetable, a train leaves every 30 minutes.

62560.q: A train on an hourly timetable leaves on the hour and takes 47 minutes to reach the next hub. How long do travellers wait there until the next full hour?
62560.e: The train arrives 47 minutes after leaving. Until the next full hour there are 60 minus 47 = 13 minutes left.
62560.m: If the journey time does not fit the timetable rhythm, there are waiting times at the hub.

62561.q: How many departures per hour in each direction does a suburban train line running every quarter of an hour have?
62561.e: An hour has 60 minutes. 60 ÷ 15 = 4, so a train leaves every 15 minutes.
62561.m: With a train every quarter of an hour, four trains run per hour.

69687.q: How many tens does the number 100 have?
69687.m: A hundred is made up of ten tens.

69688.q: How do you write “forty-seven” as a number?
69688.e: Forty is 4 tens and seven is 7 ones, so together they make 47.
69688.m: Forty-seven is written with a four at the front and a seven at the back.

69690.q: What is the biggest two-digit number?
69690.e: Two-digit numbers have two digits. The biggest is 99, because 100 already has three digits.

69691.q: What is the smallest two-digit number?
69691.e: The numbers from 1 to 9 have only one digit. The first number with two digits is 10.

69693.q: How many numbers do you say when you count from 1 to 100?
69693.e: From 1 to 100 you say each number once, which is exactly 100 numbers.
69693.m: If you count from 1 to 100, you say a hundred numbers.

69694.q: Lea has 4 ten-franc notes and 6 one-franc coins. How many francs does she have?
69694.e: 4 ten-franc notes are 40 francs, plus 6 francs: 40 + 6 = 46.
69694.m: Count ten-franc notes as tens and one-franc coins as ones.

69695.q: How do you write “three hundred and twenty-five” as a number?
69695.e: Three hundred is 3 hundreds, and twenty-five is 2 tens and 5 ones. Together that makes 325.
69695.m: Three hundred and twenty-five is written as 325.

69696.q: How many hundreds are there in 1000?
69696.e: 10 times 100 makes 1000. So 1000 is exactly 10 hundreds.
69696.m: A thousand is made up of ten hundreds.

69697.q: What is the biggest three-digit number?
69697.e: Three-digit numbers have three digits. The biggest is 999, because 1000 already has four digits.

69698.q: What is the smallest three-digit number?
69698.e: The numbers up to 99 have at most two digits. The first number with three digits is 100.

69699.q: You count in hundreds: 200, 300, 400. Which number comes next?
69699.e: When counting in hundreds, you add 100 each time: 400 + 100 = 500.
69699.m: When counting in hundreds, only the hundreds digit changes.

69700.q: How do you say the number 708 in words?
69700.e: 708 has 7 hundreds, 0 tens and 8 ones. That is why you say seven hundred and eight.
69700.m: You do not hear a zero in the tens place when you say the number.

69701.q: You count backwards in tens: 530, 520, 510. Which number comes next?
69701.e: Counting backwards in tens, you take away 10 each time: 510 − 10 = 500.
69701.m: When counting backwards, the numbers get smaller.

69702.q: Which of these numbers lies between 600 and 700?
69702.e: 650 has 6 hundreds and is bigger than 600 but smaller than 700. The other numbers have 5 or 7 hundreds.
69702.m: All numbers between 600 and 700 have six hundreds.

69703.q: How many tens does the number 58 have?
69703.e: In 58, the 5 is in the tens place and the 8 is in the ones place. So 58 has five tens.
69703.m: The left digit of a two-digit number shows the tens.

69704.q: Which digit is in the hundreds place in 472?
69704.e: In three-digit numbers, the hundreds are on the far left. In 472 that is the 4.
69704.m: In three-digit numbers, the hundreds digit is on the far left.

69705.q: Which number has 3 hundreds, 6 tens and 2 ones?
69705.e: 3 hundreds are 300, 6 tens are 60, plus 2 ones: 300 + 60 + 2 = 362.
69705.m: You write the hundreds first, then the tens and finally the ones.

69706.q: Which number has 5 hundreds, 0 tens and 4 ones?
69706.e: 5 hundreds are 500, plus 4 ones: 500 + 4 = 504. For the missing tens, you write a 0.
69706.m: If a place is empty, you write a zero there.

69707.q: How many ones are the same as 1 ten?
69707.e: You can bundle 10 ones into one ten. That is why 1 ten equals 10 ones.
69707.m: Ten ones together make one ten.

69708.m: Twelve tens make a hundred and twenty.

69709.q: What is the value of the digit 6 in the number 765?
69709.e: In 765, the 6 is in the tens place. So it means 6 tens, which is 60.
69709.m: The place of a digit decides its value.

69710.q: How many whole hundreds are there in the number 890?
69710.e: In 890, the 8 is in the hundreds place. So there are 8 whole hundreds in 890.
69710.m: The hundreds digit shows how many whole hundreds a number has.

69711.q: Which number is exactly halfway between 0 and 10 on the number line?
69711.e: From 0 to 5 is 5 steps and from 5 to 10 is also 5 steps. That is why 5 is exactly in the middle.
69711.m: The middle is the same distance from both ends.

69712.q: Which number is exactly halfway between 20 and 40 on the number line?
69712.e: From 20 to 30 is 10 steps and from 30 to 40 is also 10. So 30 is in the middle.
69712.m: Between two tens numbers, you find the middle with jumps of equal size.

69713.q: Which number is exactly halfway between 100 and 200 on the number line?
69713.e: From 100 to 150 is 50 steps and from 150 to 200 is also 50. So 150 is in the middle.
69713.m: Half the way from 100 to 200 is a jump of 50.

69714.q: Where are the bigger numbers on a horizontal number line?
69714.e: On the number line, the numbers get bigger and bigger from left to right.
69714.m: The further right a number is, the bigger it is.

69715.q: You are standing on 35 on the number line and jump 10 to the right. Where do you land?
69715.e: A jump to the right means plus: 35 + 10 = 45.
69715.m: Jumping to the right means adding.

69716.q: You are standing on 80 on the number line and jump 3 steps to the left. Where do you land?
69716.e: A jump to the left means minus: 80 − 3 = 77.
69716.m: Jumping to the left means taking away.

69717.q: Which of these numbers is closest to 50 on the number line?
69717.e: 47 is only 3 steps away from 50. 56 is 6 steps, 57 is 7 and 42 is 8 steps away.
69717.m: The number with the shortest distance is the closest.

69718.q: Between which tens numbers does the number 64 lie?
69718.e: 64 has 6 tens. It is bigger than 60 but smaller than 70.
69718.m: The tens digit tells you the ten before.

69719.q: What is the smallest even number that is bigger than 50?
69719.e: 51 is odd, and 50 is not bigger than 50. The next even number after 50 is 52.
69719.m: Even numbers follow each other in steps of two.

69720.q: Which digit tells you whether a number is even?
69720.e: Whether a number is even or odd depends only on the last digit, which is the ones.
69720.m: The ones digit shows whether a number is even.

69721.q: What do you get if you add two even numbers together?
69721.e: Even numbers are made up entirely of pairs. If you add pairs together, they stay pairs, for example 4 + 6 = 10.
69721.m: Even plus even always makes even.

69722.q: What do you get if you add two odd numbers together?
69722.e: With every odd number, one is left over. The two leftover ones together make a pair, for example 3 + 5 = 8.
69722.m: Odd plus odd always makes even.

69723.q: Is the number 0 even or odd?
69723.e: 0 can be divided by 2 with no remainder. That is why 0 belongs to the even numbers.
69723.m: Zero is also an even number.

69724.q: What is the biggest odd number that is smaller than 100?
69724.e: 99 ends in 9 and so is odd. 101 is bigger than 100.

69725.q: Two children want to share 15 sweets fairly with none left over. Why does this not work?
69725.e: Each child would get 7 sweets, which makes 14 altogether. One sweet is left over because 15 is odd.
69725.m: Odd numbers cannot be split into two equal parts with no remainder.

69726.e: Doubling means taking the number twice: 7 + 7 = 14.
69726.m: Doubling means adding a number to itself.

69728.e: Halving means splitting into two equal parts: 9 + 9 = 18, so half is 9.
69728.m: Halving is the opposite of doubling.

69729.e: 150 + 150 = 300. That is why 150 is half of 300.
69729.m: Halving makes two parts of the same size.

69730.e: 45 + 45 = 90. You can work it out like this: 40 + 40 = 80 and 5 + 5 = 10, together 90.
69730.m: You can double the tens and the ones separately.

69731.e: 35 + 35 = 70. You can work it out like this: half of 60 is 30 and half of 10 is 5, together 35.
69731.m: You can split a number into parts and halve each part.

69732.q: Mia has 12 francs. Tim has twice as much. How many francs does Tim have?
69732.m: Twice as much means two times as much.

69733.q: A cake has 8 pieces. Half of them are eaten. How many pieces are left?
69733.e: Half of 8 is 4. When 4 pieces have been eaten, 4 pieces are left.
69733.m: If you take away half, the other half is left.

69734.e: 250 + 250 = 500. Two two hundred and fifties make five hundred.
69734.m: Double two hundred and fifty is five hundred.

69735.e: You can first go up to 10: 8 + 2 = 10, then 5 more makes 15.
69735.m: When crossing ten, first go up to the full ten.

69736.e: You first go back to 10: 13 − 3 = 10, then take away 3 more to make 7.
69736.m: When taking away, you can first go back to the full ten.

69737.m: Split the number so that you reach the next ten first.

69738.e: 72 − 2 = 70, then take away 3 more to make 67.
69738.m: When taking away across a ten, it helps to stop at the full ten.

69739.e: First the tens: 35 + 20 = 55. Then the ones: 55 + 7 = 62.
69739.m: You can add the tens first and then the ones.

69740.m: You can take away the tens first and then the ones.

69741.m: You can add the hundreds and the tens separately.

69742.m: Big numbers are best taken away in steps.

69743.q: An ice cream costs 3 francs 40 centimes. You pay with 5 francs. How much change do you get?
69743.e: From 3.40 to 4 francs, 60 centimes are missing, and from 4 to 5 francs another 1 franc. Together that is 1 franc 60 centimes.
69743.m: You can work out change by counting up to the amount you paid.

69745.e: 6 times 7 = 42. You can work it out like this: 5 times 7 = 35, and 7 more makes 42.
69745.m: You can work out a hard times sum from an easy one.

69746.e: 10 times 9 = 90. Take away two lots of 9 from that: 90 − 18 = 72.
69746.m: Multiplying by ten helps with harder times table sums.

69747.e: 7 times 8 = 56. A memory aid is the sequence 5, 6, 7, 8: 56 = 7 times 8.

69748.e: 9 times 9 = 81. You can work it out like this: 10 times 9 = 90, minus 9 makes 81.

69749.e: 6 times 6 = 36. You can work it out like this: 5 times 6 = 30, and 6 more makes 36.

69750.q: Which of these numbers is not an answer in the five times table?
69750.e: The answers in the five times table always end in 5 or 0. 32 ends in 2 and does not belong.
69750.m: All numbers in the five times table end in 5 or 0.

69751.q: A bike has 2 wheels. How many wheels do 8 bikes have altogether?
69751.m: You count equal groups using the times tables.

69752.q: A week has 7 days. How many days are there in 4 weeks?

69753.e: 3 times 5 = 15 fits into 17. From 15 to 17 there are 2 more, and that is the remainder.
69753.m: The remainder is what is left over when dividing.

69754.m: Look for the biggest times sum that still fits.

69755.m: The times tables help when dividing with a remainder.

69756.m: You can check any division with a remainder.

69757.m: To check, work out four times eight plus six and you get thirty-eight.

69758.q: 19 apples are shared equally between 3 children. How many apples are left over?
69758.e: Each child gets 6 apples, because 6 times 3 = 18. Of 19 apples, 1 is left over.
69758.m: What is left over when sharing fairly is called the remainder.

69759.q: 26 children make groups of 4. How many full groups are there?
69759.e: 6 times 4 = 24 children are in full groups. 2 children are left over and are not a full group.
69759.m: Count full groups without the remainder.

69760.q: Which remainder is not possible when dividing by 5?
69760.e: If the remainder were 5, you could take away another 5. That is why the remainder when dividing by 5 is at most 4.
69760.m: The remainder must be smaller than the number you divide by.

69761.e: 5 times 9 = 45. 9 fits exactly five times into 45, and nothing is left over.
69761.m: If a division works out exactly, the remainder is zero.

69762.e: The number before is the one directly in front of it. Before 40 comes 39.
69762.m: The number before is one smaller.

69763.e: The number after is the one directly following it. After 59 comes 60.
69763.m: The number after is one bigger.

69764.q: Which numbers are the neighbours of 100?
69764.e: The neighbouring numbers are the number before and the number after: 99 and 101.
69764.m: Every number has one neighbour before it and one after it.

69765.m: After a number ending in two nines, a new hundred always starts.

69766.m: Before a full hundred comes a number ending in two nines.

69767.q: Which number is exactly between 26 and 28?
69767.e: 26 and 28 are the neighbouring numbers of 27. That is why 27 is in between.
69767.m: A number always lies between its two neighbours.

69768.q: Which number has the neighbours 549 and 551?
69768.e: The number between 549 and 551 is 550. The number before it is 549 and the number after it is 551.
69768.m: Neighbouring numbers always differ from their number by one.

69769.e: 45 has 4 tens, 54 has 5 tens. 45 is smaller than 54, so you write 45 < 54.
69769.m: With two-digit numbers, the tens decide first.

69770.q: Which of these numbers is the biggest?
69770.e: They all have three digits. 710 and 701 have 7 hundreds, but 710 has more tens. That is why 710 is the biggest.
69770.m: First compare the hundreds, then the tens and then the ones.

69771.e: 8 + 5 makes 13. Both sides are the same size, so the equals sign goes there.
69771.m: If both sides are the same size, you write the equals sign.

69772.e: With “>”, the open side is on the left. The number on the left is bigger, for example 9 > 4.
69772.m: The open side of the sign faces the bigger number.

69773.e: 20 + 30 makes 50, and 50 is bigger than 45. The other statements are false.
69773.m: Work it out first and then compare.

69774.q: Which sign goes between 2 times 6 and 3 times 4?
69774.e: 2 times 6 = 12 and 3 times 4 = 12. Both sides make 12, so the equals sign goes in between.
69774.m: Different sums can have the same answer.

69775.q: Which list is in order from the smallest to the biggest number?
69775.e: 19 is the smallest, then comes 91. The three-digit numbers 109 and 190 are bigger, and 109 is smaller than 190.
69775.m: Two-digit numbers are always smaller than three-digit numbers.

69776.e: 3 tens and 4 tens are 7 tens. 7 tens are 70.
69776.m: Work with tens numbers like ones, just with tens.

69777.e: 9 tens minus 6 tens are 3 tens, so 30.
69777.m: Nine minus six helps you work out ninety minus sixty.

69778.e: 8 tens and 6 tens are 14 tens, so 140.
69778.m: Fourteen tens make a hundred and forty.

69779.m: You can take away too much first and then add some back.

69780.m: With tens numbers, you multiply as in the times tables and add a zero.

69781.e: 6 tens divided by 3 are 2 tens, so 20.
69781.m: Sixty divided by three makes twenty.

69783.e: 10 fits eight times into 80, because 8 times 10 = 80.
69783.m: When you divide a tens number by ten, the zero disappears.

69784.q: How many tens do you need to add to 40 to get 100?
69784.e: From 40 to 100, 60 is missing. That is 6 tens.
69784.m: When making up to a hundred, count the missing tens.

69785.q: How many sides does a circle have?
69785.e: A circle has just one round line. It has no straight sides and no corners.
69785.m: A circle is completely round and has no straight sides.

69786.q: Which object has the shape of a circle?
69786.e: A coin like the 5-franc coin is round. From above it looks like a circle.
69786.m: Coins have the shape of a circle.

69787.q: What can you use to draw a nice circle?
69787.e: A pair of compasses turns around a fixed point. This makes a round line, a circle.
69787.m: You draw circles with a pair of compasses.

69788.q: Which road sign has the shape of a triangle?
69788.e: The “Give way” sign is a triangle standing on its point. The stop sign is an octagon.
69788.m: The “Give way” sign is a triangle.

69789.q: You put two identical triangles together along their long side. Which shape can this make?
69789.e: If you put two identical triangles side by side, you get a four-sided shape, for example a square or a rectangle.
69789.m: Two identical triangles together make a four-sided shape.

69790.q: How many corners does a quadrilateral have?
69790.e: A quadrilateral has four corners and four sides. Squares and rectangles are quadrilaterals.

69791.q: Which of these shapes is NOT a quadrilateral?
69791.e: The square, rectangle and rhombus have four corners. The triangle has only three corners.
69791.m: A triangle is not a quadrilateral.

69792.q: How many corners does a pentagon have?
69792.e: A pentagon has five corners and five sides.

69793.q: What is special about a square?
a: All its sides are the same length
Two of its sides are round
69793.e: In a square, all four sides are the same length. All the corners are right angles.
69793.m: In a square, all four sides are the same length.

69794.q: What is true of a rectangle that is not a square?
a: Two sides are longer than the others
All sides are the same length
69794.e: A rectangle has two long and two short sides. The opposite sides are the same length.
69794.m: In a rectangle, opposite sides are the same length.

69795.q: Which object usually has the shape of a rectangle?
69795.e: A door is taller than it is wide and has four square corners. That is a rectangle.
69795.m: A door has the shape of a rectangle.

69796.q: Which object usually has the shape of a square?
69796.e: A chessboard has 64 squares. Each one has four sides of equal length and four square corners.
69796.m: The squares on a chessboard are squares.

69797.q: A rectangle is 5 cm long and 2 cm wide. How long are all its sides together?
69797.e: You work out 5 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 14. All four sides together are 14 cm long.
69797.m: For the perimeter, you add up all the sides.

69798.q: A square has sides of 2 cm. How long are all four sides together?
69798.e: You work out 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8. All the sides together are 8 cm long.
69798.m: For a square, you multiply one side by four.

69799.q: Is every square also a rectangle?
69799.e: A rectangle has four right angles. A square also has four right angles, and its sides are the same length too.
69799.m: Every square is also a rectangle.

69800.q: A rectangle is 3 cm long and 2 cm wide. How many squares with 1 cm sides fit into it?
69800.e: 3 squares fit in a row, and there are 2 rows. 3 times 2 is 6.
69800.m: You can cover a rectangle with small squares.

69801.q: How many small squares with 1 cm sides fit into a square with 2 cm sides?
69801.e: 2 small squares fit in each row, and there are 2 rows. 2 times 2 is 4.
69801.m: You can divide a square into smaller squares.

69802.q: Which solid can roll in every direction?
69802.e: A sphere is round all over. That is why it rolls in every direction.
69802.m: A sphere rolls in every direction.

69803.q: Which of these solids cannot roll?
69803.e: A cube has only flat faces and edges. That is why it does not roll but only tips over. The sphere, cylinder and cone have round surfaces and can roll.
69803.m: A cube has only flat faces and does not roll.

69804.q: What shape is a tin can?
69804.e: A tin is round at the top and bottom and curved at the side. This shape is called a cylinder.
69804.m: A tin has the shape of a cylinder.

69805.e: A shoebox has only rectangular faces and straight edges. This shape is called a cuboid.

69806.q: Which object has the shape of a sphere?
69806.e: A football is round all over. It has the shape of a sphere.
69806.m: A football has the shape of a sphere.

69807.q: Which solid can roll and also stand flat?
69807.e: A cylinder has flat round faces to stand on. It can roll on its curved side.
69807.m: A cylinder can roll and stand.

69808.q: Which solid has six square faces of the same size?
69808.e: In a cube, all six faces are squares of the same size.
69808.m: A cube has six identical squares as faces.

69809.q: What makes a cuboid different from a cube?
69809.e: In a cube, all the faces are squares. In a cuboid, the faces can also be rectangles.
69809.m: A cuboid can have rectangular faces.

69810.q: Roughly what shape is an ice cream cone?
69810.e: An ice cream cone is round at the top and pointed at the bottom. This shape is called a cone.
69810.m: An ice cream cone has the shape of a cone.

69811.q: How many corners does a sphere have?
69811.e: A sphere is completely round. It has no corners and no edges.

69812.q: How many corners does a cube have?
69812.e: A cube has four corners at the top and four corners at the bottom. 4 + 4 = 8.

69813.q: How many edges does a cube have?
69813.e: There are 4 edges at the top, 4 edges at the bottom and 4 edges at the sides. 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.

69814.q: How many faces does a cuboid have?
69814.e: A cuboid has one face each at the top, bottom, front, back, left and right. That is 6 faces.

69815.q: How many corners does a pyramid with a square base have?
69815.e: It has 4 corners at the bottom, plus the tip at the top. 4 + 1 = 5.
69815.m: A pyramid with a square base has five corners.

69816.q: What is an edge on a cube?
a: The line where two faces meet
69816.e: Where two faces meet, a straight line is formed. This line is called an edge.
69816.m: An edge is where two faces meet.

69817.q: What is a corner on a cube?
69817.e: On a cube, three edges meet at each corner. The corner is pointed.

69818.q: How many flat faces does a cylinder have?
69818.e: A cylinder has one flat, round face at the top and one at the bottom. In between there is a curved surface.
69818.m: A cylinder has two flat, round faces.

69819.q: How many points does a cone have?
69819.e: A cone has a round face at the bottom and exactly one point at the top.

69820.q: A pyramid has a square at the bottom. How many triangles does it have at the sides?
69820.e: There is a triangle on each side of the square. The square has 4 sides, so there are 4 triangles.
69820.m: A pyramid with a square base has four triangles.

69821.q: What is a line of symmetry?
a: A line that divides a shape into two equal halves
A round line around a shape
69821.e: The line of symmetry divides a shape so that one half is the mirror image of the other.
69821.m: The line of symmetry divides a shape into two equal halves.

69822.q: How many lines of symmetry does a rectangle that is not a square have?
69822.e: A rectangle has one vertical and one horizontal line of symmetry. The lines through the corners are not lines of symmetry.
69822.m: A rectangle has two lines of symmetry.

69823.q: Which capital letter is symmetrical if you divide it vertically down the middle?
69823.e: With A, the left and right halves are the same. That is not the case with F, R and G.

69824.q: On which animal do the two wings look like mirror images?
69824.e: The two wings of a butterfly look the same, like mirror images.

69825.q: You hold your right hand up to a mirror. Which hand does your reflection seem to be holding up?
69825.e: A mirror swaps left and right. That is why your right hand looks like a left hand in the mirror.
69825.m: In a mirror, left and right are swapped.

69826.q: Can you fold the square Swiss flag so that both halves fit exactly on top of each other?
69826.e: The white cross is exactly in the middle of the red square. If you fold the flag in the middle, both halves fit on top of each other.

69827.q: How many lines of symmetry does a circle have?
69827.e: Every straight line through the centre divides the circle into two equal halves. There are infinitely many of these.
69827.m: A circle has infinitely many lines of symmetry.

69828.q: Which digit is symmetrical if you divide it horizontally across the middle?
69828.e: With 3, the top half is the same as the bottom half. That is not the case with 4, 7 and 2.
69828.m: The digit 3 has a horizontal line of symmetry.

69829.q: What comes next in the pattern: red, blue, red, blue, red, ...?
69829.e: Red and blue always take turns. After red comes blue.
69829.m: In a pattern, the same thing always repeats.

69830.q: What comes next in the pattern: circle, triangle, triangle, circle, triangle, triangle, ...?
69830.e: The pattern is always circle, triangle, triangle. Then it starts again with a circle.
69830.m: Look for the part that repeats.

69831.q: What comes next in the sequence: 2, 4, 6, 8, ...?
69831.e: Each number is 2 bigger than the one before. 8 + 2 = 10.
69831.m: In this sequence, you always add 2.

69832.q: Which shape is missing: square, circle, square, ..., square, circle?
69832.e: Square and circle take turns. After a square there is always a circle.
69832.m: You can find missing parts in a pattern.

69834.q: What comes next in the pattern: A, B, B, A, B, B, A, ...?
69834.e: The pattern is A, B, B. So after the A comes a B again.
69834.m: A pattern always repeats in the same way.

69836.q: A pattern goes: star, heart, moon, star, heart, moon. Which picture is 7th?
69836.e: The pattern has 3 parts. After 6 pictures it starts again, so the 7th picture is a star again.
69836.m: After each complete pattern, it starts from the beginning.

69837.q: You are facing forwards and turn to the right and then to the right again. Which way are you facing now?
69837.e: Two quarter turns to the right make a half turn. That is why you are now facing backwards.
69837.m: Two right turns make a half turn.

69838.q: In Switzerland, which side of the road do cars drive on?
69838.e: In Switzerland, traffic drives on the right. Cars and bikes drive on the right-hand side.
69838.m: In Switzerland, you drive on the right.

69839.q: Which hand do most people write with?
69839.e: Most people are right-handed. About one person in ten writes with their left hand.
69839.m: Most people write with their right hand.

69840.q: In Switzerland, which way do you look first before crossing a road?
69840.e: On the near side of the road, the cars come from the left. That is why you look left, right and left again.
69840.m: Before crossing, look left, right, left.

69841.q: A child is standing opposite you and raises their right hand. On which side do you see this hand?
69841.e: Someone standing opposite you is facing the other way. So their right hand is on your left.
69841.m: When someone faces you, left and right are swapped.

69842.q: In which direction do you read a line of text in German?
69842.e: In German you start on the left and read to the right.
69842.m: German is read from left to right.

69843.q: You walk north and turn left. Which direction are you walking in now?
69843.e: When you face north, west is on your left. After turning left, you walk west.
69843.m: When you walk north, west is on your left-hand side.

69844.q: Where in the chest is the heart in most people?
a: A little more to the left
A little more to the right
69844.e: The heart is in the middle of the chest, but a little more to the left.
69844.m: The heart is a little more on the left side.

69845.q: A lamp hangs above the table. Where is the table?
69845.e: If the lamp is above the table, then the table is under the lamp.
69845.m: If A is above B, then B is under A.

69846.q: Anna is standing in front of Ben. Where is Ben standing?
69846.e: If Anna is in front, Ben is standing behind her.
69846.m: If A is in front of B, then B is behind A.

69847.q: Three children are standing in a row: Lea, Tim, Mia. Who is in the middle?
69847.e: Tim is standing between Lea and Mia. He is in the middle.
69847.m: Whoever stands between two others is in the middle.

69848.q: The cat is lying right inside, and the basket is all around it. Which word fits: The cat is lying ... the basket.
69848.e: When something is inside, you say “in”. The cat is lying in the basket.

69849.q: On the shelf, the red book is above the blue one and the blue one is above the green one. Which book is at the very bottom?
69849.e: Red is at the top, then comes blue and green is at the very bottom.
69849.m: You put the things in order from top to bottom.

69850.q: 5 children are standing in a queue. Max is third from the front. How many children are behind him?
69850.e: There are 2 children in front of Max. 5 minus 3 = 2, so there are 2 children behind him.
69850.m: You can count to work out places in a row.

69851.q: The ball is lying between the house and the tree. What is true?
a: The ball is in the middle
The ball is in the house
The ball is in the tree
The ball is behind the house
69851.e: “Between” means there is something on both sides. The ball is in the middle.
69851.m: “Between” means in the middle of two things.

69852.q: A tower is made of 4 cubes on top of each other. You put 2 more cubes on top. How many cubes does the tower have now?
69852.e: You work out 4 + 2 = 6. The tower now has 6 cubes.
69852.m: You add up all the cubes in the tower.

69853.q: A wall has 2 rows with 3 cubes each. How many cubes is that?
69853.e: 2 rows times 3 cubes are 6 cubes. Or: 3 + 3 = 6.

69854.q: How many small cubes do you need for a big cube that is 2 cubes long, 2 wide and 2 high?
69854.e: At the bottom there are 2 times 2 = 4 cubes. On top there are another 4. 4 + 4 = 8.
69854.m: A cube made of two layers of four cubes needs eight small cubes.

69855.q: You build a staircase with 3 steps: 1 cube, then 2 cubes high, then 3 cubes high. How many cubes do you need?
69855.m: For a staircase, you add up the cubes of each step.

69856.q: A tower has 7 cubes. You take 3 cubes away. How many are left?
69856.m: When you take cubes away, the building gets smaller.

69857.q: You build 3 towers with 4 cubes each. How many cubes do you need?
69857.m: You can multiply towers of the same height.

69858.q: You look at a cube building from above. What can you not see well from above?
69858.e: From above you see the base. You cannot see from above how many cubes are stacked on top of each other.
69858.m: You see the height best from the side.

69859.q: A building plan seen from above shows a number on each square. What does the number mean?
a: How many cubes are stacked there
What colour the cubes are there
How many cubes the whole building has
69859.e: In a building plan from above, you write in each square how tall the tower is there, so how many cubes are stacked on top of each other.
69859.m: In the building plan, the number shows the height of the tower.

69860.q: You fold a square sheet once exactly from corner to corner. What shape do you get?
69860.e: If you fold a square along the diagonal, two triangles lie on top of each other. You see a triangle.
